Jane Ira Bloom

Jane Ira Bloom has established herself as a major player in the world of modern jazz. Her soprano saxophone sound and original compositions are well documented on her eight recordings to date, and she has been honored by Down Beat, Time magazine, and the International Association of Jazz Educators. Jane was the first composer to be commissioned by NASA and her writing has achieved a unique combination of movement, electronics and music.
She has performed with Billy Taylor, Charlie Haden, and Cleo Laine and can be seen at major festivals and clubs here and abroad.
Ms. Bloom was interviewed in Clinton, New York on March 3, 1998, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive.
We are filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. I’m very pleased to have Jane Ira Bloom as my guest here on campus. Welcome.
Thank you.
Soprano saxophonist and composer, and I recently learned that you are now in effect orbiting the galaxy. Can you tell me how that little thing happened?

Well last week I just got an e-mail from the Lowell Observatory in Arizona, announcing that an asteroid, which orbits around the sun, basically between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter, had been named after me. Asteroid 6083 Janeirabloom — with no spaces in between the names.
Tell me about your asteroid. I mean how big it is or —

I’ll tell you what the research assistant told me, who discovered it, he said it’s about three and a half miles across, it’s basically kind of a chunk of rock. It has a somewhat eccentric orbit around the sun, after its namesake, and it’s kind of new that they’re naming these things after artists. In the past they said they used to name orbiting planetary bodies and things like that after Roman and Greek gods. The research assistant said too many asteroids, not enough gods, so they turn now to naming them after other things.
Well it must be that obviously he’s listened to some of your music. Because you have managed to bring in the kind of space theme into some of your work.

Yeah. He’d listened to some of my CDs, which have a lot of titles that resonate from thematic spatial themes. And I guess when you’re sitting in the observatory late at night, you put the CD player on so he’s been listening to albums, you know, jazz albums.

As long as we’re talking about that I’ve noticed that the titles of your own tunes seem to have some significance rather than just, you know, Jane’s Blues, or things like that. And in fact when we heard you in New York you seem to have a wide range of things that may affect your compositions. For instance there was a football theme. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
NFL.
NFL. How do you get your inspiration?

Well it’s a wide, pretty wide span of interests I have. I think because I think that it’s an improviser’s job to reflect and react to their own time, that those titles reflects the scope of things that interest me today, you know, in the 1990s. And I let them affect what I think about as a jazz player. And the titles, I think of them more like I suppose the way a poet would think about them. They’re kind of like springboards for your imagination you know. I never like to explain them, I like to let the music speak for itself. But they speak of something that’s been going on in my head about why I wrote these pieces. You have to sort of take it from there.

Okay. Well there’s an almost programmatic, at least one of the tunes I heard, you had the drummer blowing a whistle and I really liked it. And it was different than obviously the typical situation which we probably will have tonight with you, where you’re kind of thrown in with musicians you haven’t played with before and it’s pretty much okay what standards do we know — which is great to hear from the pros — but to hear a rehearsed group that’s actually playing original work, I thought it was very refreshing.

Sure. Even when you do play the standards it’s always been my point of view to just kind of say something important about why you’re playing them. You know you sort of put a different spin on them because of why you’re playing them, in 1998, and it’s not 1930 or 1940 anymore. So it makes sense to me to kind of put your stamp on whatever you do.
As you did on your last album.
Oh, right.
“The Nearness.” Some of that work seems to back up what you’re saying.

Sure. No I love the music of this tradition you know. All the standards that I perform like “‘Round Midnight,” or “The Nearness of You,” or what else did I play on that one, “Lonely House,” these are beautiful melodies, jazz ballads, and I just thought it was kind of interesting to shape them in a sort of different way.
Your start in the public school system was in Boston is that right?
Um hum.
Did you have the typical experience of learning sax in the school system?
You bet.
Yeah?

You bet, yeah. A list — every student in the third grade was asked do you want to play clarinet, saxophone, trumpet, you know, I forget what it was, violin, flute, something like that, and you had to pick.
Why did you pick — or did you pick the saxophone? Was that the first instrument?
It was shiny. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
Yeah.
You know that’s very important you know when you’re nine years old. It was shiny. And it was different.
Was there much exposure in your home to music?

On record, yeah. My folks had a nice record collection around the house. I remember I used to listen to my mom’s Ella Fitzgerald record collection, some Duke Ellington, songs from the American Songbook were around, you know, things like that were around the house.
The alto sax, was that your instrument at that time?
Sure.
Stage band?
All of the above, yeah.
Yeah.
I had to go through all of it.
When was it that you decided that, you know music is going to be it for me? Was it kind of a decision that came early, junior high?

Well it was never a question in my mind that I was a musician from the earliest memories that you could have as a kid. I can remember being fascinated with musical instruments, I mean now I’m talking really early. I knew I loved music and it was clear very early on that I had a special feeling for it. I started studying piano and drums and saxophone when I was very young. And it just took a while for me to realize that that’s what I was going to do for a living. I think it was around college time. It became clear to me that that was the only thing I could do. I didn’t really have a choice. Basically you find out it chooses you.
If I don’t do music, humm, what can I do, right?
I couldn’t think of anything I could do better than play. And when I understood what it meant to be a performer and what I brought to it and what it felt like doing it.
Was there ever an indication that you might go in the classical field of music?

I remember looking at that possibility once. Because of course studying the saxophone you had to learn how to produce sound on the instrument much in the way any classical artist might study an instrument. But I don’t know, even as a kid I think I had a sense that that wasn’t for me, that the parameters for how you had to express yourself were a little too tight for me. I didn’t feel I could express myself in that genre really.
Well you know when you think of the field of classical saxophone, it would be a little tough to make a living, probably harder than jazz. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

Probably so. But you know also there was a sense, even as a kid I understood the sensibility about the freedom that was involved in expressing yourself as a jazz player. That was more in keeping I think with my personality.
Did you establish a reputation in high school as a little bit different because you were a jazz saxophone player?

Whatever I was, yeah I was definitely different. I was definitely a music jock and no question about it, I marched to a different drummer in my younger years. But I guess I just felt this passion to study music and to play, and I guess at that time that makes you different from how you spend your free time than other kids spend their free time.

What kind of experiences outside of school in that particular area were you able to find? Because obviously you have to get out and play with people other than just the stage band. Were there opportunities to do that for you?

Yeah, you know, a suburban underground, playing in a lot of basements with friends and jazz groups in suburban basements you know. And I remember joining, forming bands, I remember well geez, let me think about this, I belonged to a Massachusetts Youth Wind Ensemble where I got a lot of interesting experience just playing in a big ensemble. That wasn’t a jazz group per se but invaluable experience learning about what it means to put musicians together to make music. I think my real training ground as a player happened when I got to college, when I was in New Haven. Because that’s when I really started to work playing in clubs and putting on concerts of original music. That’s when it started to happen was really in college.
This was at Yale?
Um hum.
Were you a music major at Yale?
Yeah I was kind of Liberal Arts, but a music major such as it was.
But you went out of your way to push your own work out there as much as you could.
Yeah.
Outside of the music department?

Yeah. It existed completely. It had nothing to do with the music department. There was a really vibrant jazz scene that was going on in New Haven in the mid-70s. It just happened that a lot of now very highly regarded jazz musicians, you know, and very innovative ones, all happened to be in New Haven at that time.
Like whom?

Oh gee, Anthony Davis, George Lewis, Gerry Hemingway, Mark Dresser, Leo Smith, Bobby Naughton, Mario Pavone. It was an interesting time. These are all very highly regarded jazz artists, and interesting innovative thinkers too, and they all happened to be there at that one time. David Mott — I mean all kinds of people. So there were a lot of © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

musicians around, a lot of opportunities to play with like-minded players, and we created a scene there, at the clubs and the concert scene. So there was a little burst of activity in New Haven during the 70s. And it was I guess my training ground.
I wanted to ask you about when two things happened for you. First of all, the soprano saxophone — when did that become your instrument of choice?

Well you know I think I was studying with Joe Viola in Boston, a very fine saxophone teacher. And soprano was a passion of his. So I can remember him pulling it out during lessons and stuff. I started with him when I was about 12 or 13, so I was exposed to it quite young. And when I heard him play it, I liked that. I want to play like that.
Was it a straight one?
Yeah, sure. And I’m sure I picked up a lot of love for the instrument from him. So I started studying with him I think I was 12 or so, 12 years old, 13, I think it was 12. So that’s when it began.
When were you able to get one?

Well I rented one early on. Then I remember I had a, I think it was a Czechoslovakian one, it was a Maadi or something. And then it didn’t take long before I wanted a Selmer. So I had got myself a Selmer alto and that took some time, then a Selmer soprano. Actually the instrument that he picked out for me, way back then, is the same one I’m playing. I mean I have other ones at home, I have three of them now, but that’s my main horn still.
The other question I had was composing your own music is obviously very important to you. Did you have a time, can you remember the first time you wrote your own tune?

I was very young. I started studying piano, I think I was about four or five, four. And unlike other kind of classical early piano study, I began early on improvising and not knowing it. And I had a teacher who would show me what chord changes were and how to write things out, so that even when I was beginning to study the piano, I was also improvising at the same time. I didn’t know it. So my learning process went hand in hand, you know, improvising and studying written form as well. So it was not like it was anything exotic to me, it was just a part of what I did. And I think that’s why it seems so intuitive to me to do it.
It’s fortunate that you had a piano teacher that could give you a little support in that area.
Yeah. Harvey Steinberg. I’ll never forget him.
Thank you Harvey. You know because too often you hear the stories about people taking piano lessons and they want to try doing their own thing and it’s like, don’t do that.

Don’t do this don’t do that. No, music was pure joy for me. There was never anything associated with music other than pursuing a passion with a vengeance. I never had any bad experiences like that in my music education. I had terrific teachers and was very © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
fortunate I think to live outside of Boston where I had access to a lot of great music training.
What was your experience at Berklee like?

Well I was a private student of Joe’s. Joe Viola’s. I was just a private student. I never studied there. But I used to sit in the hall and listen to all the students there talk about whatever. And Joe occasionally used to sneak me into an ensemble or something like that, to give me a little experience or a sax quartet or a sax section or something. But by and large my association was with Joe Viola. He was the head of the woodwind department there and my goodness I studied with him for a long, long time. A long apprenticeship.
Did he use the keyboard to teach you improvising? I’ve always been curious as to how people teach improvising, if they don’t provide some kind of harmonic set-up.

Well you know we would work on improvising but he didn’t teach me per se. He gave me the tools for learning how to do it, but he used to play the chords, he used to plunk out the chords on the piano and I’d blow some choruses on various standard tunes, things like that. But learning how to improvise, that’s something — you really learn how to do it on your own. Nobody teaches you how to do it. They just sort of create the settings for you to experiment in. I think Joe approached it that way. And he gave me the tools for trying to hear and reach the things that I wanted to be able to play.

This is a tough question I think, but I’ve often liked to see if I can tell what people think about when they improvise. Are you conscious to a great degree of the changes as they go by or is it a little more esoteric than that?

Well here’s the way — I’m not entirely sure. When I study a piece of music that has important harmonic material in it, I internalize it. I think this is how a lot of jazz musicians would describe the process to you, but I play it over and over and over again, both on the horn and on the piano, until the coloristic changes that are in the tune aren’t symbols on a page anymore, they’re inside. I can hear them in their fullness, in their harmonic fullness, where they exist in a structure. And if I’ve succeeded in really learning that tune, the page goes away and the tune is then inside me. And occasionally I may have the chart in front of me and you use those symbols, the chord symbols as little reminders of what’s going on. But like I said I think if you really know the tune, the harmony is inside you and also I think the melody is, on some unconscious level, being sung in my head when I’m playing. It’s there. It’s inside. And I think that’s some kind of guidepost that exists in your musical imagination at some deep level. I don’t know it’s hard to talk about this stuff. But I have a sense that that’s what it’s about. Because when I’m trying to teach students and things about it, that’s the way I describe it to them.
I told you it was a tough question. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
It is.

It’s hard to talk about it. But in fact a couple of things you’ve said right now, I saw yesterday when you were working with some of the students, in that while they were soloing you decided to play the melody of the tune behind them.
Right. To help them.
To help them feel their way through the song.
It’s kind of like putting on training wheels. You know? Here it is, remember? And let them just dance on top of it, to help them remember where the structure is.

You had mentioned yesterday, I heard you talking about how you feel it’s really important for teachers, jazz teachers to be seasoned performers when possible. Do you think that there is stuff about jazz education today that doesn’t follow that?

You know I’m a bad one to talk to about jazz education, because it’s not really my métier to even know exactly what’s going on. My sense is that because I was an experiential learner and because I know what I know, with the guidance and input of a lot of theory and things like that, but I know that I learned what I learned by doing. So that’s kind of my slant on what it takes to be a player. So I haven’t really been in the jazz education environment that much. My path has not been as a teacher so far, in the 20 years I’ve been out there. I’ll do the occasional master classes and things like that, but my path has really been as a performer. So I hope I have something to give from that experience that’s a little bit different.
Did you ever have an experience where you got into like almost an old fashioned cutting session?
A long time ago.
Yeah.

Like I was saying to the students yesterday, I don’t believe that jazz is a contact sport you know; that students should be frightened into how difficult it is to learn how to play jazz. Yes it’s difficult but it’s a beautiful experience if you have this passion for this thing, and when you share it with other people. So yeah you know there’s a good healthy amount of ability in all of us as players and we put it out there for people to see at times, but I don’t believe the most constructive musical settings come about because people are cutting each other on a bandstand. I mean it’s most like a sports spectacle than it is a musical endeavor.

Well there’s a — I don’t know if it’s small or large, whatever — movement for women in jazz. Has it ever felt to you like you have been at a disadvantage or at an advantage because you were a woman playing jazz?

No easy answer to that question either, that’s a big one. There are both sides to the equation. When I began playing in the early 70s, there was a lot of consciousness in the © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

air about women’s issues. There were a lot of women’s jazz festivals that sprang up that I played at, and I got exposure through, that had they not been there I might not have been heard. But they were the one venue that I saw a possibility to play, and at that point in time I’d play anyplace, anywhere, anytime. So there was something beneficial about that environment at that time. Disadvantages? It’s been my point of view that things haven’t changed as much as I had hoped they would in 20 years. You know when I first started playing I thought things would be a lot better, the playing field would be a lot more equal than I see it today, and mostly in respect to the business environment of jazz. Because there are plenty of women players who are now out there, and they’re playing horns and they’re playing drums and bass, all the rhythm instruments, all the things that were not considered instruments for women to play in jazz, they’re out there playing them now. But the thing that kind of is upsetting is that when I talk to some of these younger women, I’m still hearing some of the same stories I remember listening to 20 years ago about social acceptance and business acceptance. So it has gotten better but boy, not as quickly and not as much as I had thought.

You had talked, yesterday I overheard you talking about recording albums and the business of finding labels and you had mentioned that the business for records these days is not too healthy in the jazz world and that the time you’re getting to make records is getting smaller.

Yeah. Well this is the middle, the jazz trenches, we’re not talking about the major jazz labels, we’re talking about all the independent jazz labels that live and operate in this kind of middle ground, on very small budgets. And the fact is it’s become so easy to make a CD now, everybody can make one, anybody can make a CD and get it out there and reproduce it and get it in the record stores. And I’m not entirely sure what that says about the quality and the content of what’s in those CDs if they’re so easy to do, how carefully we think about what it is that we record and want to put out there. There is also a lot of other entertainment options for people who buy CDs now, you know the computer and internet has changed all kinds of things. And entertainment options people have, not just listening to records. People can barely listen to 60 minutes of music, they don’t have that amount of time. An LP used to be 40 minutes. People could handle that. Jazz critics say today that they don’t even have time to listen to an entire CD when they’re evaluating new albums. It takes a lot of time.
Yeah. You get a stack of CDs on your desk that you’re supposed to review and each one of them is an hour.
Yeah. It also brings up the point of, you know, how carefully are you thinking about what you are recording, how special you want to make those musical moments.
Are you a fan of technology? © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
Yeah.
You are.

Yeah. Live electronics are an important part of my music, and something I’ve always been interested in, something I’ve never been afraid of or ever thought that it was any kind of contradiction to the life and thought of a jazz musician. It’s just interesting to me.
Yeah. How did that first happen? To say hey, this is cool stuff here.

I think I was just always interested in electronic music, got exposed to it in college, met musicians in New York who were a little more technically minded than I was, taught me about how to use effects processing. There was an electronics music studio in New York that was set up to help musicians get access to new equipment called PASS, Public Access Synthesizer Studio, which now has turned into Harvest Works.
Oh I’ve seen that, yes.

At the time, we’re talking 15 years ago, a very interesting place because that’s a place where I learned, I got a chance to learn about how to handle and work around with electronics and get a feel for it. And now, well the whole world of computers and electronics has changed drastically since then, but it was my introduction.
Does it add to the time you need in the studio to take advantage of the electronics that you want to?

Well if I bring my own live electronics set-up, you have to spend a lot more time setting it up, making sure that all the lines are clear and all the things that can go wrong won’t go wrong. So it gets a little more — it’s not that bad, but just a few more input lines. You have to sort of make sure everything is A-okay.
Right. Well you seem to have pretty wide ranging tastes. And you were the first person commissioned by NASA to write. How did that come about?
A letter.
You just got a letter?

I wrote a letter to NASA in the early 80s. I was just fascinated with whether NASA had ever thought about the future of the arts in space. I was very interested in what zero gravity might mean to the future of artistic performance. You know if there wasn’t gravity, how might music and dance and sculpture and theater, how all these things might be different. So I wondered whether NASA might have ever thought about it too. I wrote them a letter and six months later I got an envelope back from a gentleman named Robert Schulman, who is head of the NASA art program. I didn’t even know that this existed. And he was an avid jazz fan to boot. And I corresponded with him for years. And eventually our correspondence came up with the idea of how about commissioning the first musician instead of a visual artist to be part of this NASA art program. Basically they would invite you down with special access to go see a launch, a landing, and to tour © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

the various NASA facilities, to see things people never get to see. And it was an extraordinary experience. And from that experience you contribute a work of art to their traveling space art collection. And I wound up composing a piece for chamber orchestra and jazz musicians that got performed at the Kennedy Space Center in 1989, and involved six jazz musicians inside the orchestra, it involved live electronics that I used, and a sound surround speaker system. So it had all kinds of interesting new elements to it. It kind of foreshadowed work that I did later on in my own work.
That must have been exciting.
Oh it was probably one of the highlights of my life, definitely.
What launch did you see by the way?

STS 26, which was the first return to flight launch after the Challenger accident. It was an exciting time, yeah. I got to meet a lot of interesting astronauts, I met astronaut John Young, shook hands with a man who had stepped on the moon. He actually spoke and gave a beautiful speech about the future of the arts and music in space, before we did the concert. It was quite wonderful.
You also had a piece performed at Carnegie Hall, isn’t that right?

Yeah. That was like a further incarnation of some of that NASA work. Basically that was a piece called “Einstein’s Red/Blue Universe,” and it was played by The American Composers Orchestra, a very fine new music orchestra in New York, conducted by Dennis Russell Davies, and it was my first piece for full symphony orchestra and jazz musicians, and sound surround brass choirs in the Carnegie Hall balconies. It was the funniest thing. We had — in order to maximize the use of the musicians there are points in the score where the brass section has to leave the stage and get up to the balcony in the Carnegie Hall. And that’s pretty precipitous up there by the way. They had to take the elevator to get up there in the middle of the piece.
You had to write the time into the piece for how fast the elevator is going up.

Yup, yup. And then there were also some very carefully orchestrated movement aspects in the piece for the brass sections and woodwind sections in the orchestra. Movement, almost these doppler like movement effects, is very much a part of my kind of intuitive playing style. And over the years, through working with dancers and things, I got interested in orchestrating it, trying to notate it so other musicians, actually whole sections of instruments, could sort of use my original impulse and also move their horns in this doppleresque kind of way to create these timbre shifts. So if you can imagine whole trumpet, trombone and brass sections standing up with bells in the air, and turning 180 and 360° in different directions and different speeds, in unison, to create these kind of spherical soundscapes I guess you could call it. And it’s been a passion of mine, an interest. It came all about from working at NASA. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
Did the people in the orchestra, like how did they handle that?
This is a tremendous new music. There’s nothing these guys can’t do.
Because they’re used to new—
Yeah. And they were very generous with their time and their creativity, and they did it.
Tell me, were you really nervous with that premier?

Oh sure. Are you kidding? I mean I’ve stood in front of an orchestra as the soloist, you know like in a classical sense, but with all these other things going on, there’s actually a danger element in this music. I had a choreographer friend come in, just to help teach the brass players how to move and play at the same time without getting dizzy, how not to hyperventilate. This is a new, new technique you know.
God forbid one of them went the wrong way too.
Naa, these were pros, these were professionals.
And were you playing also in this piece?
Oh yeah, yeah. I was like the featured soloist with the improvising jazz musicians, who were still inside the orchestra, but toward the front.
Right. Have you ever had an occasion to — a situation somewhat like that — where you weren’t involved in the playing at all, that you just were maybe in the audience or in the wings?

In my writing for film I have, yeah. Film and television and things like that. I’ll write for instruments, not my own saxophone, it’s not called for. And that’s been a wonderful experience, because you get to work with musicians who still have extraordinary feeling and how to communicate that to them, just on the page or with words.
Do you get to see the film beforehand or is it somewhere along the way you actually get to see the footage that you’re writing behind as it happened?

Oh of course. Oh yeah you live with it. If you’re lucky you get to live with it for a while. But often it’s quick, they give you two or three weeks with it. But yeah you spend a lot of time just looking at it, feeling the rhythm of it.
In its sequence of it, you know that you have, let’s say 30 seconds to do a certain thing and then you have to hit a cue?

Sometimes you have to mark it yourself with the director. You have to go through the cues, and kind of figure out where is the most effective place for music, and that’s a learning process too, and each director has their own feel for that that you have to sort of work with.
You did a film with — Brian Dennehy was in that?

Yeah. He has a tremendous gift for music. He sat down and he knew exactly where the musical energy should be and where it should be directed. It was quite wonderful to work with him. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
And your husband is Joe Grafasi? Did I pronounce that right?
Yeah.
And being that he’s an actor, both of you are in professions that can be a little perilous at times I would think.
Well we’re both performers. We understand what that means. The lifestyle and the travel and what it means to really prepare yourself for performance. We understand that about each other.
Without getting too personal, has there ever been a time where you’ve both had a stretch of a month or so where the work seems to be down?
I’m sorry, say it again?
Your work flow. I imagine being that you’re both basically self employed, it’s kind of up and down.
Sure.
Does it ever happen where you’re both like down?

Of course, sure. It’s just in the natural flow of events. But you know you have faith. If you’ve been doing it long enough eventually something’s going to happen. But sure there’s been all kinds of matches, you know I’m up, he’s down; he’s up, I’m down; we’re both up; we’re both down. All possibilities exist in the life of artists.
Have you both lived in — New York has been your base?
Yeah I’ve been there about 20 years.
Has it ever occurred to you that you’d want to go somewhere else?
I can’t think of where else I could be. It’s where my whole family is from to be honest. And it’s where I feel I have to be musically. I don’t know, I couldn’t think of any other place at the moment.
But you had said that as far as playing right in New York, do you play a lot in New York?
Here and there. It’s not as frequent as you would think. But the work is generated often because I’m there, which is a strange kind of contradiction but that’s just the way it is.
What’s the competition like? Let’s suppose you’ve got a good quartet of people and you’d really like to get them into the Iridium or something. How do you go about that?

Well your reputation has to speak for itself. I mean your recordings and the recognition that you get through them, and your playing and your acceptance among the jazz community and the music business community. Usually that has a lot more to do with it than the acceptance among the music community, the music business community. And then you have to have a solid reputation about what you do and I think time helps, people know and see your body of work over a period of time.
Do you call the club yourself? © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
No, no, no, no. You always work through representatives when it comes to that kind of thing.
Right. They don’t want to talk to the artists.
No, no.

I mean I was interested one day to pick up the book from the New York — I guess it’s 802, the Local, and look at the number of saxophone players in there. It’s like how do all these people work? I suppose some of them are part timers.
There’s a lot of musicians that aren’t even in that book. Yeah there’s a lot of great musicians in New York City. That’s what makes it the interesting place that it is too, so yeah.
Does the musician’s union have a part in what you do at all?
No. No I don’t have much to do with it at all.
It used to be I guess really quite powerful.
Yeah. Not so anymore. Not particularly in the underground jazz world.
Have you ever done any of the big band opportunities, or pit work?

No. I did that when I first came to New York and I had a very bad experience, and when I left college I was asked to join the Mercer Ellington Orchestra. I went on some road trip with them to New Jersey. I was still in music school at the time. And I just didn’t think that that was the direction for me. I know that’s a way that many instrumentalists apprentice before they find themselves in the world of jazz, but I followed a different path, I really did. I just didn’t think that that was going to be musically helpful to me at that time. And so I went it alone.
To get your own stuff played, it must be imperative that you have a core of people that you try to work with as much as possible, as we saw at the IAJE.
Yeah, and it changes from time to time too, but yeah a body of musicians who get inside your work.
Is it hard to keep a core of people to provide enough work for them?

Sure. And often you have a number of people, not just one bassist who you work with but several, and likewise rhythm sections, so that you’ve sort of worked on your music intimately with a number of musicians so that you’re not locked into just one or two people. Although when you really want that special feeling there are certain people that do a certain thing a certain way, and no other people can do that, or no other chemistry of a group of people can do it the same way. So you get used to understanding that.

You’ve been able to — in addition to having your own band — played with quite a list of people, and I wonder if there’s been some folks that have stood out in your mind as being really memorable experiences. © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

Oh a lot. And for different reasons too. Working with Cleo Laine — some kind of special feeling I had about playing with her, and it meant a lot to me. Playing with Charlie Haden and Ed Blackwell was probably the most exciting rhythm section I’ve ever worked with in my life, and I played the Village Vanguard with them. I mean I will never forget Blackwell, ever. I think Ed Blackwell, of the instrumentalists, Ed Blackwell probably had a more profound influence on me, absolutely, not because we talked about anything, but completely musically. It was just completely about music communication of what he did and what I played with him, and what happened when we played, that I’ll never forget. I don’t think I’ve ever felt a cymbal like that in my life again, since he passed away.
Was that a fairly spontaneous gig too?

Well I recorded with them on Enja Records in the early 80s. And it was a recording that I was asked to pick whatever rhythm players I wanted to record with and they were them. And it included pianist Fred Hersch and a number of festival appearances and concert appearances happened after that recording. It was called “Mighty Lights” and at the time it got a lot of attention, and the most exciting for me, opportunity, was to play a week at the Vanguard with this group. So I always remember that.
I guess. I understood you did “Piano Jazz” with Marian McPartland?
Sure. And I interviewed with Billy Taylor. I mean I’ve been through it. You know, been through it. Ups and downs you know.
Did you ever have a point where you felt like, man this is just too hard. I can’t do this anymore.

Sure you say that to yourself sometimes. One of the times when I was feeling like that was when I wrote that letter to NASA. And look what happened. Somehow you pull yourself up, somehow. And the music pulls you up you know. Anytime you just play, that’s the kind of magic that makes you want it more, and you keep striving for that moment again. That’s what we live for. It’s in the music I think that gets you through all that hard stuff.
Did your parents support you in your eventual choice to become a jazz musician?

Well you know I think I was kind of a mystery to them, what it was that I was doing. But you know I’m sure they were happy that I was doing what I wanted to do. That was probably the most important thing to them. They didn’t entirely understand it but you know that’s the way it goes.
Are they still with us?
Yeah.
And how does your mother describe to other people what you do?
I don’t know you’ll have to ask her, you’ll have to ask her. © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

That’s interesting. When you hope to make a record, do you have a number of labels that you’re working with? How does the opportunity to record come about. I know you’ve done seven or eight over the years.

At the moment I’m with Arabesque Jazz. And it’s nice having an association with a jazz record label that’s interested in pursuing having you record a number, not just one, but following your career and to have you continue to record on their label as you develop. So that’s been a nice relationship. Over the years I worked — oh I was with CBS for about four years, and I was with Enja Records and JMT Records. It’s very common you know for jazz musicians to record wherever they can.
And they approach you. Do the small labels approach you?
Yeah. You get to meet them at various times.
Yeah. Was there any advantage to being with CBS as a larger label?
Sure. Are you kidding?
It’s a rhetorical question.
Yeah. I mean talk about distribution, yeah, obviously a whole lot more people become aware of your work because of its visibility. Absolutely.
Do you ever have to buy your own recordings back from the labels?

I haven’t done that but a small jazz label bought the masters from CBS when they turned into SONY you know, and has re-released those two CBS albums under the Koch Jazz label. So I’m very happy to have them out there because otherwise they would be sitting in a vault somewhere in New York. So great — that’s great that happens.
Getting back a moment to your compositions, do you write at the piano, at a keyboard?
Yup I do, most of it. Sometimes ideas come to me on the horn, but for the most part, yeah I’m a piano thinker.
Do you have any kind of set-up in your apartment, a four track or any of that kind of gear?
All of the above, yeah. Yeah I’ve got a synthesizer keyboard and a JB 1080 which is a beautiful orchestral — a synthesizer with a lot of orchestral sounds on it. All kinds of tools to help.

Do you ever take a tune — you had mentioned the orchestral sounds and everything — you find a really great sound on the synthesizer, it’s really lush and it’s got all kinds of reverb and the whole thing — is there a danger in building a composition around a sound like that, that the melodic and harmonic content of the music may be kind of light? Do you ever take things back to the piano and see, does this thing stand on its own?

Oh absolutely. I mean if you’re a composer, the musical impulse comes from here. It’s not in your hands, it’s not in the sound. I think that’s what you’re getting at. The same criticism is often made about using electronics, it’s like a black box. That it dictates what © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

you do. But I think if you’re a true compositional thinker, the ideas come from here and translate through your use of sounds and whatever. But you should be very much in control of the musical materials, no matter what tools you’re using, whether it be a synthesizer or electronics or whatever, which are just as valid as playing an acoustic instrument, you know, it’s just how you do it, how you do it.
Who do you like to listen to these days? Who or what?
I was thinking last week I was listening to Ali Akbar Khan play North Indian Sarod.
Oh everybody listens to that sure.
Different stuff, no, different stuff. Not what you would think too. And I have my Frank Sinatra albums, the Capitol years. It’s pretty eclectic, pretty eclectic.
Are there saxophone players out there these days that you go out of your way to hear?
Oh there are a lot of good players, yeah. I mean for me to like itemize, to say this person or that person, that’s not important, but sure there are a lot of great players doing interesting things.
What’s the immediate future for you as far as upcoming gigs, concerts?

Museum of Modern Art in New York this coming month. Continuing to play with my trio with Bobby Previte on drums, Cameron Brown will be playing bass and sometimes Mark Dresser plays bass. Finishing a recording for Arabesque that’s coming up this spring, I’ve been doing some quartet recording, that also involved Fred Hersch on piano, Mark Dresser on bass and Bobby Previte on drums. This was the group that played Sweet Basil’s last year, and just raised the bandstand it was so wonderful. Anyway, what else am I up to? Planning a tour for January 1999, this is how far in advance the real world of jazz musicians has to think, I’ve been invited to play at the Melbourne Jazz Festival and the Sydney Jazz Festival in Australia, and preparing and find funding to get over there and do all that. All kinds of things are in the air.
Are you able to take your own group when you go?

Take a trio. Yeah take bass and drums with me. Planning a concert at the Einstein Planetarium down at the National Air and Space Museum. That’s also in the works probably for the fall. I mean it’s not like the old days where you get a gig and you show up, next night — lot of long term planning’s involved in being a jazz musician now. Different, huh?
Yeah, different, and also calculating what you have to charge in 1999 — in January of 1999 to go to Australia, what’s a fair price for me to ask to go over there.
Oh and it varies from country to country, yeah. A whole lot of factors. You have to be a business person as well as a musician and a lot of things, a lot of balls you’ve got to keep in the air.
You and your husband. Constantly juggling. © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-
Sure. Sure. It’s life in the arts.
I forgot to ask you about your Pilobolus. That must have been fun, huh?

Well I met the Pilobolus Company in 1979 when I lived in New Haven and they worked out of Connecticut. So one of the dancers, Allison Chase, became aware of my work and she wanted a solo saxophone score for her new solo piece that she had done, it was later called “Moonblind.” So we spent a lot of weeks working in her studio. I loved it. And I didn’t realize at the time how much I loved modern dance and working with dancers. And as time moved on, when I got to New York, I started working with an improvisational dance company, which was run by a choreographer named Richard Bull. And I spent many years performing with them, not only as a player but learning how to play and move at the same time with the improvisational dancers. It was some very bold stuff. And I think again it was kind of like an experience that I jumped off from, learning about playing and moving and why I’m interested in how sound changes when it moves, and not being afraid of the physical aspect of myself as a player, kind of becoming more conscious of it, more aware of it, more interested in it. Because the dancers were fascinated with it. Musicians might go huh, but the dancers were just fascinated and they helped me you know. So over time my work with Pilobolus, I did the “Moonblind” piece for them early on, late 70s, and a couple of years ago I orchestrated a piece for the full company called “The Doubling Cube” which they’re now performing on tour all over the world, so it’s on tape and it has a lot of drums and saxophone and bass on it too, as well as some electronic sounds.
It must be a thrill to write something that has some longevity to it like that, that goes out and is spread around.

Yeah. Well that’s how you think about records too. You know you don’t realize what a life they have after you’ve given birth to them. They go out into the world and affect people in ways you never know, sometimes not until 15 years later.
Like the astronomer.
Yeah, right.
Do you listen to your own work much?
No.
Never?

Just keep doing something that you hope is better. You keep wanting to do something different. Ask a musician what they’re most interested in, it’s what they’re doing right at the moment you know. That’s what interests you.
Is Joe a good critic of your work?
Sure. It goes both ways. It goes both ways yeah. We see inside each other pretty well. © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-
Have either one of you ever done a gig or — how shall I phrase this — that turned out to be really like oh man, I wish I hadn’t done that?

Sure. Oh there’s always those things that happen. Absolutely. At least you have somebody to commiserate with. It happens, yeah. Sure. There are always events that happen that, oh just, this was a hard one or something like that. But you know, you just, you know you’ve got to pick yourself up and keep moving on, because if you’ve been at it long enough you realize that there’s always another day you know, there’s always another chorus, there’s always another opportunity to play another improvisation that’s going to make that one go into history.
Right. Help keep things in perspective. The high is that much higher I guess.
Yeah. It’s just time that teaches you that. You can get upset but it doesn’t last for too long.
Would you suggest to someone who is just in high school and has aspirations to be a jazz musician, would you have any advice for them?

Play as much as you can. Whatever opportunity you have to perform, take it. The whole idea is you can’t learn how to improvise without doing it, and hopefully every day you know. That’s how you learn how to do it and do it well. So take every opportunity you can to play and play with musicians who might be better than you are, to learn from them, and take any opportunity you can, even when it’s scary.
In New York is there any kind of racial scene connected with jazz that is uncomfortable or is there any issues about race these days in the music that you’ve been able to see?

Well if you were to look, as time has gone on, whether the music community has been polarized into black and white, I’ve felt that a lot, when it did exist, and when I saw it, it seemed like it was the musicians who are not in control of it, it felt like the music business community, the promoters, the club owners, were having more input into this, and the critics as well too I think, than I think the musicians. And that was a scary moment, a scary perception. That choices were being made about who musicians would play or not play with, based not on musical reasons, but something else. I remember there was a period, I remember talking with Billy Taylor about this in that interview, it probably wasn’t on the Charles Kuralt show, but I remember we had an interesting discussion about this. And he was very concerned about it too.
That there was control being exerted from—

Subtle. This is covert. I mean we’re not talking about overt stuff. It was covert pressure in terms of what was accepted in the club and what was considered the right thing and all black groups or all white, whatever it was. It was as if the musicians were not in control in deciding what they thought was best for their own musical development, who they should play with or who they shouldn’t. That was the real issue. © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-
Who was trying to control it?

Oh it’s not a who, it’s not any particular person, it was prevalent in, you could see it in the way festivals and the way groups were lining up to play at certain clubs at certain places, and the way they were being recorded too. It’s not a finger pointing thing. It was — you could sense it in the consciousness of what was going on, and it had to do with also the kind of conservativism that had overtaken the music community as well too. I think it went hand in hand with what was going on with it in the country. In the class I spoke to here at the college we were talking about gender issues in music, and Dr. Woods brought up the fact that what was going on in the music community was reflecting what was going on in the society and the conservativism of the culture at the time as well. And I think there’s something very true in that.
Has the music been affected by the fact that it’s become almost institutionalized, that mostly it’s taught in colleges now as opposed to kind of on the job training?

It definitely will change the nature of what that music is, how you learn it. I suppose that’s why I’m even more adamant, even having come from a college environment, but knowing deep in my heart that that’s not how you learn how to play. It’s really through experience so you have to take the best from both worlds is my advice to any students who are going through a music education whatever, a formal music education. But there’s something to be said for both those approaches and how you use it as a player, composer, whatever. Take everything you can but you have to do it.

Well you’ve certainly been doing it. I know Down Beat has recognized you as a top instrumentalist on your instrument. Are you bothered at all by — let me start again with that — contemporary jazz, where they put Kenny G and a few other folks in the jazz bins, do you think that that term is healthy for the music?

I don’t know. Words don’t mean that much to me. I don’t think about it that much with that kind of perspective who they call jazz or not jazz. Is it important or isn’t it? It’s a hard question. I have to kind of plead — from the view of most performing musicians, our concentration is really on doing the thing. I don’t sit around thinking about that, you know to be honest.
You’re doing your own thing.
Doing it.
And promoting it.
No not just that but you know that’s not, yeah, it’s just not where my attention is, it’s not where I put my energy into thinking about.
Okay. That’s a good answer.
Yeah, it’s true you know. You know Kenny G can do whatever he wants you know. © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-
Right. Well I want to thank you for your time today, and I hope that if I haven’t asked you anything that you had on your mind —

Well let me think about that for a minute. Well you know here’s something, this is interesting, I mean to put on a videotape. Because when you have these kind of talks and you’re trying to talk about music and get these issues sort of out, it makes it seem as if it’s clear what you do and what you think. I think I always like to make sure that after I have one of these experiences that whoever I’m talking to — you at the time — or whoever’s listening to this videotape, that the words that were used to describe what we do help us understand things but it’s not the thing itself. And I always worry that talking so much about it may demystify something about the ambiguity of what we do. It’s so, I am sitting here trying to put it into words but it doesn’t exist in that realm in my mind. And so it’s like a conscious effort to talk to you about it. I’m using a different part of my brain to do it, and the part of my brain that plays music and lives in that music world. And I guess I always like to just leave with the thought that it’s much more ambiguous and abstract and emotional and passionate thing that we’re talking about than these words convey. And that’s why we play instead of talk.
The answer in on your records not in talking about them. Yeah.
Yeah.
Well that’s a good statement to make and I’m glad you said that, that talking about it only goes so far. Do you have any other passions besides music? Hobbies?
Photography. I’ve been in to black & white photography since I was teenager and I kind of re-discovered it this past couple of years. So a lot of time I spend in the darkroom.
Neat.

Tai Chi. I practice Tai Chi and I’ve been studying Tai Chi for two years and I find it very complementary to things I think about musically. And again it gets in line with my feeling about the physicalness of things that I feel, you know the old sound body, sound mind, you know, when I’m physically aware I feel mentally aware too for playing and clear, empty, you know what I mean, to play. So I think there’s a relationship between physical disciplines and musical too.
Good advice also. Think we’ll ever see one of your photos on one of your CDs?
Maybe the next one.
All right. I’ll look forward to that. You have recording plans coming up?
Yeah. I think things will get underway I hope this spring yeah.
Is it hard for you to — let’s say you have a record date coming up and you’re able to do six of your own tunes. Is it hard for you to pick six? Do you have that much material of your own?
Always. © Fillius Jazz Archive -21-
That you say I want to do all this?

There’s more than enough material to keep recording for a long, long time. That’s not a problem. That’s not a problem. It’s just when I make a record I like to think about recordings, like I said, in a special way. I like to think about how they make a statement from beginning to end. In the old days they used to call it kind of thematic albums, but even if there’s some you know kind of thread in my own mind, about some kind of concept I’m trying to get across, you know, in everything that this music states in an album, so it’s not just about cut, cut, cut you know. Here’s a song, here’s a song, here’s a song and we’re going to splice them together you know. I try to think about an album as a curve from beginning to end, and what connects it and what I’m trying to say with each statement. And hopefully that makes it the kind of album that you want to listen to not just once, but many times, and after five or ten or fifteen years it might be worth listening to again, if the values on it are strong enough.
Good thoughts.
A different approach you know.
All right. Well you have some things to do later on today, and —
Yeah. Nice talking to you.
— here on the campus and thank for your time and I’m sure we’ll be hearing some great things about you in the future.
Thanks.
All right. © Fillius Jazz Archive -22-
